q-98336:
A simple closed curve is positively oriented if, when traveling along it, one always has the curve interior to the left and the curve exterior to the right. Otherwise, the curve is negatively oriented. 

A curve is positively oriented if it is traversed counterclockwise and is negatively oriented if it is traversed clockwise.

q-70649:
Remember that the equation of a sphere centered at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ with radius $r>0$ is given by

$$
(x-{x}_{0})^{2}+(y-{y}_{0})^{2}+(z-{z}_{0})^{2}={r}^{2}.
$$

We can write our equation as

$$
{x}^{2}+(y-(-5))^{2}+{z}^{2}=(\sqrt{10})^{2},
$$

which gives us the center at the point point $C(0,-5,0)$ and the radius $r=\sqrt{10}.$

q-164249:
Remember that the equation of a sphere centered at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ with radius $r>0$ is given by

$$
(x-{x}_{0})^{2}+(y-{y}_{0})^{2}+(z-{z}_{0})^{2}={r}^{2}.
$$

By completing the square for the variable $y$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-4z & =12 \\ (x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}+({z}^{2}-4z+4) & =12+4 \\ (x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}+(z-2)^{2} & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can write our equation as

$$
(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}+(z-2)^{2}={4}^{2},
$$

which gives us a radius of $4.$

q-73215:
To find the $z$-intercepts, we plug $x=0$ and $y=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(0-3)^{2}}{12}+\frac{(0-1)^{2}}{8}+\frac{(z-2)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{(z-2)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{7}{8}+\frac{(z-2)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(z-2)^{2}}{2} & =\frac{1}{8} \\ (z-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ z-2 & =\pm \frac{1}{2} \\ z & =2\pm \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the solutions $z=\frac{3}{2}$ and $z=\frac{5}{2}.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $z$-axis are $(0,0,\frac{3}{2})$ and $(0,0,\frac{5}{2}).$

q-71118:
To find the $z$-intercepts, we plug $x=0$ and $y=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(0+1)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(0-2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{11} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{4}+\frac{4}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{11} & =1 \\ \frac{{z}^{2}}{11} & =\frac{11}{36} \\ {z}^{2} & =\frac{121}{36} \\ z & =\pm \frac{11}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the solutions $z=-\frac{11}{6}$ and $z=\frac{11}{6}.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $z$-axis are $(0,0,-\frac{11}{6})$ and $(0,0,\frac{11}{6}).$

q-164310:
From the equation of the sphere, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}+{z}^{2} & =5 \\ {z}^{2} & =5-((x-2)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}) \\ z & =\pm \sqrt{5-((x-2)^{2}+(y+2)^{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the square root is defined only for non-negative arguments, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5-((x-2)^{2}+(y+2)^{2})\ge 0 \\ (x-2)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}\le 5\end{aligned}
$$

This inequality describes the interior and boundary of the circle 

$$
(x-2)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=5
$$

which is a circle of radius $\sqrt{5}$ centered at $(2,-2)$ in the $xy$-plane.

q-164399:
From the ellipsoid equation, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(z-5)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ (z-5)^{2} & =2(1-(x-1)^{2}-\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{4}) \\ z-5 & =\pm \sqrt{2(1-(x-1)^{2}-\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{4})}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since the square root is defined only for non-negative arguments, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-(x-1)^{2}-\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{4}\ge 0 \\ (x-1)^{2}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{4}\le 1\end{aligned}
$$

 

which gives the interior of the ellipse $(x-1)^{2}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{4}=1$ and its boundary.

Therefore, the domain is 

$$
{(x,y)\,:\,(x-1)^{2}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{4}\le 1}.
$$

q-70926:
To find the intersection of the sphere and the plane $x=2$, we substitute $x=2$ into the equation of the sphere:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2)^{2}+(y+4)^{2}+{z}^{2} & =16 \\ 4+(y+4)^{2}+{z}^{2} & =16 \\ (y+4)^{2}+{z}^{2} & =12 \\ (y+4)^{2}+{z}^{2} & =(2\sqrt{3})^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Projecting this onto the $yz$-plane gives us the circle of radius $2\sqrt{3}$ centered at $(-4,0).$

q-164179:
To find the trace in the $xz$-plane, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the sphere:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(0)^{2}+(z-1)^{2}=2 \\ {x}^{2}+(z-1)^{2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

q-128445:
First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0) & =\frac{1}{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+0+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the level curve that passes through $P(1,0)$ is the $\frac{1}{2}$-level curve.

Recall that the level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=\frac{1}{2}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level curve that passes through $P(1,0)$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$

q-36434:
First, we find the value of the function at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,2) & =\frac{1}{2-{1}^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the level curve that passes through $P(1,2)$ is the $1$-level curve.

Recall that the level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=1.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ \frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}} & =1 \\ 1 & =y-{x}^{2} \\ y & ={x}^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level curve that passes through $P(1,2)$ is the parabola $y={x}^{2}+1.$

q-129062:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =c \\ {y}^{2} & =c({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) \\ c{x}^{2}+(c-1){y}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=0,$ the level curve is the line $y=0,$ which is the $x$-axis. So, I is false.

- If $c=1,$ the level curve is the line $x=0,$ which is the $y$-axis. So, II is false.

- If $c=2,$  then we obtain 

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=2\,⟹\,2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=0.
$$

However, the only real solution to this equation is  $(x,y)=(0,0),$ which is not in the domain of $f(x,y)$ because it would result in division by zero. Thus, III is false.

So, the correct answer is "None of the listed".

q-71398:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2y} & =c \\ {x}^{2}+2y & ={c}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=0$ then the level curve is $y=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},$ which is not a circle.

- If $c=1$ then the level curve is $y=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},$ which is not a hyperbola.

- If $c=2$ then the level curve is $y=2-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},$ which is a parabola.

So, only statement III is true.

q-129116:
The level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equations 

$$
f(x,y)=c.
$$

Notice that the range of $f(x,y)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ So, we will consider level curves for any value of $c.$
Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(y-x) & =c \\ y-x & ={e}^{c} \\ y & =x+{e}^{c}.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above gives us a family of lines with slope of $1.$ Also, note that ${e}^{c}>0$ for all $c.$ Therefore, the correct graph is as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14098720/assets/c115999648577bfb60015f0e54dd0c6d6de22076e87026ba94c49e56207144e0.png)

q-129112:
The level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equations 

$$
f(x,y)=c.
$$

Notice that the range of $f(x,y)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ So, we will consider level curves for any value of $c.$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ y-x & =c \\ y & =x+c.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above gives us a family of lines with slope of $1.$ Therefore, the correct graph is as follows:
